title: Business Breakdown

sections.title: Don't build without a plan
bullets: Imagine building a house with no blueprint. You just show up every day and wing it.
You watch a random YouTube video for today's task, and you run to Home Depot 40 times a day.
Nobody would build a house that way. But if you're here, I suspect that's exactly how you've been building your business.
Not anymore. Here's the big picture of what you're building:
**Qualified leads:** a steady flow of customers who are ready and able to pay market rate for the services you offer.
**Five-star work:** consistent, quality service that earns five-star reviews, repeat jobs, and referrals to friends and family.
**A good job for everyone:** a consistent, quality job for every employee, including you, the owner.

sections.title: Your business is a house
bullets: The framework I use has three parts: the foundation, the pillars, and the roof. Each part has its own course.

**Documentation and data (foundation):** every process is written down clearly enough that someone else could follow it without calling you, and you track the numbers that tell you how it's going. That's Get It Out of Your Head.

**Four pillars, built to CODE:** a house needs four corners to stand, and so does your business. The pillars go in order, the same way every customer moves through your business: Capture, Obtain, Deliver, Extend.
**Capture:** get people's attention and bring in leads. Every page and post has a clear call to action.
**Obtain:** turn those leads into paying customers. You answer frequently asked questions quickly and the same way every time. Capture and Obtain are Book the Right Customers.
**Deliver:** do great work and give customers a great experience. Your services are defined and limited, and every job is done the same great way. That's Same Great Job, Every Time.

**Extend:** keep the relationship going after the job is done, with the four Rs. Refine: ask every customer for feedback, then use it to get better. Review: ask happy customers for a 5-star review. Refer: ask happy customers to send friends and family your way. Repeat: be the one they call next time, whether that's a maintenance plan or their next job. That's Customers for Life.
**Brand (roof):** a consistent brand and social media presence, so what people expect from you is what they get, every time. It covers the whole house.

sections.title: Plan the work, work the plan
bullets: There are thousands of things you could be doing every day.
There's a never-ending stream of content with new ideas and things you MUST do, and the sense of urgency is intense.
Instead, slow down and focus. Build a sound structure first, then add the amenities.
Save the ideas, the things you think are cool, and the things you want to learn to your Idea Bank. More on that in the next lesson, Own Your 24.

sections.title: Brick by brick
bullets: You don't build the whole house at once. You lay one brick at a time.
Keep the house in balance, so no pillar gets ahead of the others.
Work on one area at a time. Whichever part of the house is lagging behind is your next project.

sections.title: AI is a power tool
bullets: If you're not using AI, you're building this house with hand tools.
You use a drill to install a cabinet. The drill doesn't install the cabinet.
You use a circular saw to cut a 2x4. The saw doesn't cut the 2x4.
AI helps you build. It doesn't build for you.
Every course teaches AI the same way you probably learned to use power tools: hands-on.

summary: What we're building, before we build it: the plan for your business, laid out as a house. It's the picture every other course builds toward.
takeaways: Don't build without a plan. You're building a business with qualified leads, five-star work, and a good job for everyone in it, including you.
Your business is a house: a foundation, four pillars built to CODE (Capture, Obtain, Deliver, Extend), and your brand as the roof.
Plan the work, work the plan. Build the structure first, and save new ideas for later.
You build it brick by brick, one area at a time.
AI is a power tool. It helps you build. It doesn't build for you.

action.title: Set up your Claude
action.text: Two steps. First, sign up for Claude Pro at claude.ai (or upgrade if you're on the free plan). Then start a new chat, paste in the prompt below, and answer three quick questions. Claude writes a short intro about you and walks you through your settings. It takes about 15 minutes.
action.prompt:
I just signed up for Claude Pro. Help me set up my account so you know the basics about me. Keep it quick and easy. I'm new to this.

Before the first question, tell me two things:
- I can type my answers, or tap the microphone in the chat box and just talk.
- There are no wrong answers. Everything we set up today can be changed later, whenever I want.

1. Ask me three quick questions, one at a time. For questions with options, show clickable choices if you can. If not, number the options so I can answer with numbers. Always include "Other" so I can type my own answer.
- What's your name, and what do you do for work?
- I can help with almost anything. Which of these would you like help with? Pick all that fit: Work, Running my business, Home and family, Money and budgeting, Health and fitness, Learning something new, Other.
- How would you like me to talk to you? Short and to the point, Step by step with explanations, Friendly and casual, Other.

2. Write a short "about me" from my answers: three to five sentences, in plain language. Keep it general. Put it in a code block so I get a copy button, and tell me to click Copy (or select all the text and copy it) so I can paste it in the next step. I'll set up separate projects later for the areas I picked. After you write it, remind me I can update it anytime, like adding new areas once I'm more comfortable.

3. Walk me through my settings one step at a time. Wait for me to say "done" before the next step. If my screen doesn't match what you describe, ask me for a screenshot.
- Instructions: where to paste my "about me" (Settings, then Your Claude, then Instructions). Remind me to paste it in and save.
- Memory: what it does, in one sentence, and how to turn it on.
- Capabilities: which ones to turn on and which to leave off, with one line on why.

Finish with a quick checklist of what we set up.

title: Own Your 24
summary: You only get 24 hours a day. Find the one thing holding your business back, pick one project to fix it, and park every other idea until it's done.
takeaways: You only get 24 hours a day. Own them by working on one project at a time.
Find your constraint: the part of your business that breaks first. Fix that, not everything else.
Most fixes hurt. Make the hard call and get through it in months, not years.
More or better beats new, 98 times out of 100.
Every other idea goes to the Idea Bank, and fallback tasks keep you moving on the bad days.

action.title: Set up your first project
action.text: Start a new chat, paste in the prompt below, and answer six quick questions. Claude writes your project instructions and walks you through setting up your first project. It takes about 15 minutes. Next up: Job Site Prep.

helper.label: Watch me do it: set up a project

action.prompt:
I want to set up my first Claude project: a home base for my business, so every chat in it already knows how my business works. Keep it quick and easy. I'm new to this.

Before the first question, tell me two things:
- I can type my answers, or tap the microphone in the chat box and just talk.
- There are no wrong answers. I can change any of this later, whenever I want.

1. Ask me six quick questions, one at a time. For questions with options, show clickable choices if you can. If not, number the options so I can answer with numbers. Always include "Other" so I can type my own answer. For questions without options, show a short example answer. If I skip part of a question, that's fine; move on.
- What's your business called, and what's your trade? (Example: "Smith Plumbing, plumbing.")
- What's your role? Owner, and I'm in the field most days; Owner, and I mostly run the business; Owner, a bit of both; Office manager or admin; Other.
- What are your main services, and the towns or areas you cover? Is there anything you don't do? (Example: "Roof replacements and repairs, gutters. Around Tacoma. No commercial.")
- Which tools do you use for your business? Pick all that fit: Housecall Pro, Jobber, ServiceTitan, QuickBooks, Google (Gmail, Calendar, Drive), Microsoft 365 (Outlook, Word, Excel), Paper or spreadsheets, Other.
- When you write to my customers, how should it sound? Pick all that fit: Friendly and down to earth; Short and to the point; Professional; Like a quick text from me, not a corporate email; Other.
- Here are the rules I'll always follow. Do you want to change or add anything?
  - Anything I write for your customers is a draft. If your email is connected, emails land in your drafts folder so you can review them and send them yourself.
  - I'll never ask for card numbers, passwords, Social Security numbers, or bank account numbers.
  - No em dashes (the long dash that makes writing look like AI wrote it).
  - When I write to customers, I use plain words, no jargon or hype, and sound like you, not a big company.

2. Write my project instructions from my answers, with these short sections: My business, My role, My services, My tools, How to write to my customers, and Rules. Use plain language. Put it in a code block so I get a copy button, and tell me to click Copy (or select all the text and copy it) so I can paste it in the next step. Then remind me I can update it anytime, like adding a new service or tool.

3. Walk me through setting up the project one step at a time. Wait for me to say "done" before the next step. If my screen doesn't match what you describe, ask me for a screenshot.
- Create a new project and name it after my business.
- Paste my project instructions in and save.
- Start a new chat inside the project and say hi, so I can see it already knows my business.

Finish with a quick checklist of what we set up, and remind me to start every business chat inside this project from now on.

sections.title: Own your 24
bullets: There are 24 hours in a day, and we have to own them.
At least half of them go to doing the actual work. You also have your family, your health, and your responsibilities at home.
So the hours you have left for building the business count. Don't spend them on countless courses, new systems, and getting pulled in 200 directions.
"People only see the choices you made, not the options you had." You can't see focus. You just see winning. (Alex Hormozi, quoting his business partner, on The Diary of a CEO.)

sections.title: Find your constraint
bullets: Your constraint is the part of the house that's lagging behind the others. Fix anything else and nothing much changes.
**The test:** if twice as many calls came in tomorrow, what would break first? That's your constraint.
**Start with the big split:** are you short on customers, or short on people and time to do the work? Most businesses are short on customers.
Here are the common ones, from Alex Hormozi's podcast The Game (episode 894), retold for home service:
**Not enough leads or sales:** there aren't enough leads, or you're not closing them.

**Poorly defined customer:** you serve two kinds of customers (residential and commercial, budget and high end), and the one you're worse at serving is holding back the one you're better at. Pick one.
**Missing data:** you don't know, because you don't have the numbers. Set up a way to capture them. Or, if trying it and failing is faster than gathering the data, make the decision.
**Wheels falling off the bus:** you added a second crew or location, moved your best tech to run it, and now you have the same revenue with twice the overhead. You got ahead of your talent.
**No profit:** pay better, get more and better techs, and do more jobs. Or the opposite: you pay so much that you don't make money. Profit is a discipline.

**Underpriced:** you're fully booked, everyone's happy, and you're not making money. Raise your prices. You'll lose some customers and replace them with better ones. More on this in Book the Right Customers.

**One and done:** every customer buys once and you never sell to them again. Treat past customers as your best leads: maintenance plans, the next service, and referrals. More on this in Customers for Life.

sections.title: Sucks to suck
bullets: Most constraints come with a fix that hurts: drop a customer type, close the second location, change how you pay people, or raise prices.
Or you have to do things you don't like, or aren't good at.
You can waffle for 10 years, or squeeze that pain into 6 to 12 months. Lean into the hard call. It gets you out faster.
Not deciding is a decision too. It just keeps you stuck.

sections.title: More or better beats new
bullets: You've found your constraint. Now decide how to loosen it, and take time to think it through and plan before you dive in.

Loosen one constraint and a new one shows up. It's like a Rubik's Cube: fix one thing and four more pop up. Or a pendulum: fix demand and the leads pour in, so now you're short on time and techs. Fix that, and you need more leads again.
**Is your idea a new thing?** First ask: can you do what you already do 20% better? If yes, work out how and do it. If not, ask why not. That may be your real constraint.
**Not a new thing?** Ask: can you do more of what you already do? If yes, work out how and do it. If not, ask why not.
**Only if you truly can't do more or better** should you look at something new. And unless you're bringing home $1 million a year, the answer is still more or better.
98 times out of 100, your project will be more or better of something you already do.
**Before you commit, ask:** What does it cost up front, in time and money? What does it cost to keep up? Can it be automated or delegated quickly? Can one project fix two or more problems?

sections.title: The Idea Bank and fallback tasks
bullets: Work on your project, and only your project.
**The Idea Bank:** every other idea that comes up gets saved there, so you don't lose it and you don't chase it mid-project.
**Bad days:** we all have them. You can push through, but sometimes you have 30 minutes between jobs and you just can't.
**Waiting:** sometimes you've done your part and you're waiting on someone else before the project can move forward.
**Fallback tasks:** for those times, keep a short list of tasks that keep you productive and keep your momentum, like documenting a process, logging ideas, or clearing your email.
You'll build your Idea Bank and fallback list in the next lesson, Job Site Prep.

title: Job Site Prep

sections.title: Context
bullets: Claude only knows what you tell it.
Ask it to "send the invoices for the work I did yesterday," and it has no idea what work, which customers, or where your invoices live.
That's why your work project helps. It carries who you are and how your business runs into every chat, so you never start from zero.

sections.title: What is AI? Deterministic vs. probabilistic
bullets: **Deterministic:** a formula returns the same answer every time. 3 + 5 = 8, today, tomorrow, and a thousand times in a row.
Material + labor + overhead = total job cost. That's deterministic. Calculators and spreadsheets are tools that give you quick, exact answers.
**Probabilistic:** the output is a prediction, a best guess. AI predicts the most likely answer based on the context you give it.

Ask it the same question twice and you may get two different phrasings, and both are correct. That's not a defect. It's what lets AI draft, summarize, rephrase, and match your tone in a way no formula can.
They're good at opposite things. A formula can't write an email. AI can't be trusted to calculate a security deposit to the penny.

Both take information in and put something out, and both are useful tools. The main difference is whether being "creatively wrong" is OK. For a formula, wrong is a bug. For AI, a different but valid answer is expected.
**The best setup uses both, plus a human check.** Deterministic first: if this, then that. Estimates, payment terms, costs, warranties, guarantees, and answers to customer FAQs.
For example: if we install a 30-year roof, a 5-year workmanship warranty is included. If we install a 50-year roof, it's 10 years. If we make a roof repair, no workmanship warranty is included.
Then AI drafts the email that answers the customer's question. You review it quickly, edit if needed, and send.

sections.title: Easier to read: structured data and Markdown
bullets: **Structured data** means the AI knows where to look for the information it needs.
A spreadsheet is structured. A Word doc usually isn't. Bullet points are structured. A long paragraph isn't.
**Markdown** is a simple way to format text, compared to PDFs, Word docs, and the like.
It's become the main way humans, websites, and AI communicate. It's the easiest way for you and AI to understand each other.

sections.title: Notion
bullets: I'm asking you to set up Notion.
This is where Claude will start recording your SOPs, projects, and decisions.
As we go, you'll see the pages are full of structured data, and the whole thing is written in Markdown.
That lets you and your team work with Claude as effectively as possible.

summary: What AI actually is, why context matters, and why we keep everything in Notion. Then you prep the job site: Claude builds the frame of your business in Notion.
takeaways: Context: Claude only knows what you tell it. Your work project carries that context into every chat.
A formula gives the same answer every time. AI gives its best guess. Use each for what it's good at, and check AI's work.
AI works best with structured information: tables, bullet points, and Markdown.
Notion is where Claude records your SOPs, projects, and decisions.

action.title: Job Site Prep
action.text: Three steps, about 15 minutes. When you're done, Claude has built the frame of your business in Notion: Claude: Read First, your Dashboard, SOPs, Customer FAQs, Tech Stack, Brand Guide, Metrics, and Skills.

steps.title: Sign up for Notion
steps.text: Go to notion.com and create a free account. The free plan is all you need. Name your workspace after your business.

steps.title: Connect Claude to Notion
steps.text: In Claude, open Settings, then Connectors, find Notion, and click Connect. Allow access to your workspace.

steps.title: Run the prompt
steps.text: Open your work project in Claude, start a new chat, and paste in the prompt below. Claude builds the frame. It takes about 10 minutes.

helper.label: Watch me do it: steps 1 and 2

action.prompt:
I want to set up my business home base in Notion. Think of it as the frame of a house: we build the structure now and fill in the rooms later, one project at a time. Keep it quick and easy. I'm new to this.

Before we start, tell me two things:
- I can type my answers, or tap the microphone in the chat box and just talk.
- There are no wrong answers. I can change any of this later, whenever I want.

1. Connect Notion. Check if you can reach my Notion. If you can't, walk me through connecting it one step at a time (in Claude: Settings, then Connectors, then Notion, and allow access to my workspace). Wait for me to say "done." If my screen doesn't match what you describe, ask me for a screenshot.

2. Build it in my Notion. Don't ask me anything else; just build it and tell me as you finish each part. Keep it plain and simple. Pages you leave empty get one line at the top saying what they're for.
- A top page called "My Business HQ."
- Under it, "Claude: Read First": the page you read at the start of every session. Write this on it:
  - "At the start of every session": read this page (the Rules, Current state, and the three newest Session log entries), then open the Dashboard and look at the Current Project and its open Project Tasks, lowest Order first.
  - "At the end of every session": add a Session log entry at the top with today's date, what we did, and what's next. Update Current state if things changed. Keep Project Tasks true: mark what's done and add what came up.
  - "How we work":
    - One project at a time. The Current Project stays on the Dashboard until every "done when" check is done. Then we pick the next one from the Idea Bank together.
    - Project Tasks is only for the Current Project. New ideas go in the Idea Bank, with the date and why.
    - On a bad day, or while waiting on someone, pick a Fallback Task.
    - When we figure out how something gets done, it goes in the right SOP page: Capture, Obtain, Deliver, or Extend.
    - When a customer asks a question, it goes in Customer FAQs with an answer, an email template, and its Stage.
    - Tools go on the Tech Stack page. Skills go in the Skills table.
  - "Rules":
    - The rules from my project instructions.
    - Ask before deleting anything or making big changes in Notion.
    - If you're not sure where something goes, ask me. Everything has one home.
    - Ask me one question at a time, and keep it short.
    - Date everything you add.
  - "Current state": "Business HQ is set up. Next: load my first project."
  - "Session log": add today's date: "Business HQ set up."
- Under it, "Dashboard," with:
  - "Current Project": a project name and a "done when" list, left blank for now.
  - A "Project Tasks" table with columns Task, Order (1 is next), and Status (Open, Waiting, Done).
  - An "Idea Bank" table with columns Idea, Added (date), and Why.
  - "Fallback Tasks": an empty list.
- Under it, "SOPs," with four pages, in this order: "Capture" (how customers find me), "Obtain" (from first call to signed job), "Deliver" (how every job gets done), and "Extend" (feedback, reviews, referrals, and repeat customers).
- Under it, "Customer FAQs": a table with columns Question, Answer, Email Template, and Stage. Answer is the basic answer. Email Template is a ready-to-send reply when a customer asks that question. Stage shows where in the process the question comes up, and a question can have more than one: Capture, Obtain, Deliver, Extend.
- Under it, "Tech Stack": the tools I use, what each one is for, who uses it, and where the login is kept (never the password itself).
- Under it, "Brand Guide": how my business looks and sounds.
- Under it, "Metrics": the numbers I track to see how my business is doing.
- Under it, "Skills": a table of my Claude skills, with columns Skill, What it does, and File (the skill's file or a link to it), so you can find them in Notion.

3. Give me the link to "My Business HQ." Then write one line for my project instructions in a code block so I get a copy button: "My business runs from my Notion page My Business HQ. Read Claude: Read First first, then the Dashboard." Tell me to click Copy, then walk me through adding it to my project instructions one step at a time. Wait for me to say "done."

Finish with a quick checklist of what we set up. Remind me that this is just the frame, and we'll fill in the rooms one lesson at a time. I can change anything later.

title: Lay the Foundation

sections.title: See what's really going on
bullets: Before we can fix, improve, or grow this business, we need an accurate understanding of what's going on right now.
This lesson is short. It's mostly action.

You're going to backfill your SOPs. It's a bigger prompt than usual: Claude asks you a lot of questions, you answer them, and it documents your answers in Notion, so you get a clear view of your business.

How are you getting customers, and where are they coming from? How are you turning leads into jobs? How are you doing on getting paid? Are you asking for reviews? What numbers are you tracking, if any?

sections.title: Messy is fine
bullets: Don't worry about how it should be done. Answer honestly about how it's done today.

If you don't have written processes, the answer will probably sound like this: "Most of the time we do it like this. That's how it's supposed to go, but really we do it that way about half the time. The other half, someone texts me and I just do the job. Sometimes I forget to invoice. Usually it's not on the schedule, and nobody knows what's going on."
That's the reality for most one- to three-person operations. A little chaotic? That's OK. If we didn't have this problem, we wouldn't be doing this.
From there, we pick one thing at a time to improve. There's nothing wrong with your business as it is. It could just be a little better.

summary: Before you fix anything, get an honest picture of how your business runs today. Claude interviews you and writes it all into your Notion.
takeaways: Before you can fix, improve, or grow your business, you need an accurate picture of what's going on right now.
Write down what actually happens, not what should happen.
Messy is normal. That's why we're cleaning it up, one thing at a time.

action.title: Backfill your SOPs
action.text: Open your work project in Claude, start a new chat, and paste in the prompt below. Claude interviews you about how your business runs today, one area at a time (Capture, Obtain, Deliver, Extend), and writes it into your SOP pages. Skip anything. Stop anytime and pick up later.

helper.label: Watch me do it: backfill the SOPs

action.prompt:
I want to document how my business runs today, so you know how things actually work. Not how they should work. How they actually work, right now.

Before we start, tell me three things:
- I can type my answers, or tap the microphone in the chat box and just talk.
- I can skip any question. We'll come back to it later.
- Messy is fine. If something is chaotic or done differently every time, that's exactly what we write down.

First, read "Claude: Read First" in my Notion page "My Business HQ."

We'll go one area at a time, in this order: Capture, Obtain, Deliver, Extend.

How to interview me:
- Ask one question at a time. Keep questions short and plain.
- Give options to pick from when it fits, and always include "Other." For open questions, show a short example answer.
- Ask up to ten questions per area. If an answer is vague, ask one follow-up for details.
- If I say "skip," move on and note it as "Not documented yet."

What to ask about:
- Capture: How do I find customers today? Where do leads come in: website, texts, emails, phone calls, or all of them? Do I go to networking events? Do I post on social media? How do people find out my business exists?
- Obtain: How does a lead turn into an estimate, and an estimate into a job? Who does each step? When does it go into my systems, if it does? How does my pricing work? Do I offer any warranties or guarantees?
- Deliver: What services do I offer, and what don't I do? Push me to be specific. Then, once a customer says yes to the estimate: How does the job get scheduled? How does the work get done? Is there a checklist? When do I take before and after photos? How do I check the quality? When does the invoice go out? What happens if they don't pay, and who follows up?
- Extend: Do I ask customers for feedback, and do I use it? Do I ask for reviews? Do customers send referrals? Do they call me again, or sign up for a maintenance plan?

After each area:
1. Write it up on that SOP page in My Business HQ. Write it how it is, in my words, in the order things happen. Don't write what you wish it was. If it's messy or done differently every time, say so. List anything I skipped under "Not documented yet."
2. If a customer question came up, add it to Customer FAQs. If a tool came up, add it to Tech Stack.
3. Show me a short summary and ask if anything's off. Fix it.
4. Ask if I want to keep going to the next area or stop for today.

When we stop, add a Session log entry on "Claude: Read First" with today's date, which areas are done, and which are left. Remind me I can run this prompt again anytime to pick up where we left off.

title: Nerd Alert (bonus)
summary: Optional. Plain-English answers for the AI words you'll hear, the key terms this course is built on, and free resources if you want to go deeper.

sections.title: Vocab
bullets: **AI (artificial intelligence):** software that can read, write, and answer questions in plain language.
**LLM (large language model):** the technology behind Claude. It learned from an enormous amount of text, and uses those patterns to draft, summarize, and answer.
**Claude:** an AI assistant made by a company called Anthropic. You type or talk, and it answers.
**Model:** a version of Claude, like Opus, Sonnet, or Haiku. Some are faster, some are smarter. For this course, use Opus 5.5.
**Prompt:** what you ask Claude to do. A good prompt says who you are, what you want, and the details.
**Token:** the small chunks AI reads text in. One token is about three quarters of a word.
**Training data:** the text a model learned from. It's why Claude knows general facts but nothing about your business until you tell it.
**Knowledge cutoff:** the date a model's training stops. It may not know about anything newer, unless it can search the web.
**Markdown:** a simple way of writing formatted text with symbols, like # for a heading. Skills are written in it.

sections.title: Key Terms
bullets: **Context:** everything Claude knows during a chat: your project instructions, your files, and the conversation so far. The right context gets you better answers.
**Context window:** how much Claude can keep in mind at once. Very long chats run out of room, so start a fresh chat for each new task.
**Iteration:** the second and third ask. The first answer is a starting point; telling Claude what's off is where it gets good.
**Hallucination:** when AI says something wrong, confidently. That's why you check its work, especially numbers, prices, and codes.
**AI slop:** generic, unedited AI writing that sounds like it came from anywhere. Context in, your edits out, and nobody can tell.
**Drafts only:** anything Claude writes for a customer is a draft. You read it, and you send it yourself.
**Guardrails:** the limits you set on what AI does on its own, like drafts only and no personal information.
**Personal information:** customer names with phone numbers or addresses, card numbers, passwords. Keep it out of your chats.
**Project:** a home base in Claude with instructions and files, so every chat already knows your business. (Own Your 24)
**Connector:** a link that lets Claude read another app, like Notion, email, or your calendar. (Job Site Prep)
**Skill:** saved instructions Claude follows when you ask, like /boss. (/boss and Custom skills)
**Automation:** work a tool does for you on its own, the same way every time, once you've proven how it should be done.

title: SOP Basics

sections.title: Why document
bullets: If it's all in your head, you can't take a day off, get sick, or step back. The business is you.
You're documenting for future you: you on a busy day, a tired day, or six months from now when you've forgotten how you handled it last time.
Documented means consistent. Same job, same way, every time. That's what customers experience as quality, and what earns you the reviews.
It makes training easier. Hand the new guy the process instead of having him follow you around for weeks.
You can't fix what you can't see. Once it's written down, the gaps show up.
It's how you get out of the work: you can't automate or delegate what isn't documented. And a business that runs on documented processes is worth more if you ever sell.

sections.title: What to document
bullets: **Systems:** the tools and setup behind the work. Your tech stack (which tool runs each step, from lead to paid), your brand guide (just note what you have for now; we'll build it in Book the Right Customers), and billing: your price book and your chart of accounts.
**SOPs:** how the work actually gets done.
**Data:** your customers, your jobs, and the handful of numbers that tell you how the business is doing. That gets its own lesson, Data Integrity.
The rule: document how it runs today, before you change anything. You can't improve what you haven't captured.

sections.title: SOPs are simpler than you think
bullets: You don't need a giant binder. An SOP is how your business does things, written clearly enough that someone else could do it too.
**The process** is the whole thing, beginning to end.
**Procedures** take you through each step. When you get to the job: set up the site, take pictures, put your signs out.

**Scenarios** are the if-thens that throw off your procedures: materials running late, the wrong color shingles, a customer who wants to reschedule, a bounced deposit. Think of them as the questions your crew asks you over and over.
You don't need to imagine every scenario. If it's happened twice, document it. Once is a surprise. Twice is a pattern.

sections.title: Four processes run your business
bullets: They go in order, the same way every customer moves through your business. Think CODE, like building to code.
**Capture:** how leads find you and how they reach out.
**Obtain:** the appointment, the estimate, and getting it signed.
**Deliver:** scheduling, ordering materials, doing the job, invoicing, and getting paid. The job isn't delivered until you're paid.

**Extend:** the four Rs. Refine (ask for feedback and use it to get better), review (ask happy customers for a 5-star review), refer (ask them to send friends and family your way), and repeat (be the one they call next time, from a maintenance plan to their next job).

sections.title: Where to start
bullets: Start with your sales flow, then service delivery. Everything else builds on those.
Here's a roofing job: a lead comes in, the appointment, the estimate, they sign, schedule the job, order materials, the crew does the job, invoice, paid.
That's the ideal version: what happens when nothing goes wrong. Always start there.
Then write the procedures for each step, and add scenarios as they come up.

action.title: Map your sales flow
action.text: Open Claude, paste in this prompt, and answer its questions the way you'd explain it to a new guy on the crew. Typing or talking both work. Claude writes up your process at the end.
action.prompt:
I run a [type of business, for example roofing] business. I want to document my sales process, from the moment a lead comes in to the moment I get paid.

Interview me one question at a time. Start with how a new lead first reaches me, then walk through each step in order: the appointment, the estimate, getting it signed, scheduling, ordering materials, doing the job, invoicing, and getting paid. Use plain language. If my answer is vague, ask a follow-up. Skip any step I don't do.

When we've covered every step, write it up as:
1. The process: a numbered list of steps, beginning to end, with who does each step and what tool they use.
2. Gaps: any step that depends only on me, or that I do differently each time.
3. Scenarios: any "if this happens, then do that" situations I mentioned along the way.

Keep it simple enough that a new crew member could follow it.

summary: Why to document your business, and what to document: your systems, your SOPs (process, procedures, and scenarios), and your data.
takeaways: If it only lives in your head, the business can't run without you.
Document three things: your systems, your SOPs, and your data.
An SOP comes in three shapes: the process, its procedures, and scenarios.
Four processes run every business: Capture, Obtain, Deliver, and Extend.
Start with your sales flow, the ideal version, before anything else.

title: Your first skill: /boss
summary: Add /boss, the skill that runs your work sessions: it catches you up, works your current project one task at a time, and logs where you left off.

sections.title: What a skill is
bullets: A saved set of instructions Claude follows when you ask for it.
Instead of finding and pasting a long prompt every time, you just say the word.

sections.title: Meet /boss
bullets: Say "boss" and Claude opens your Dashboard and reads where you left off.
It asks how much time you have, then works your current project with you, one task at a time.
When you stop, it writes a note in your session log, so next time picks up right where you left off.

When everything on the Done when list is finished, it helps you pick the next project from your Idea Bank: what it costs up front and every month, how you'll measure it, and whether it fits your brand.

sections.title: When the list is empty
bullets: Turn your inbox into reply drafts.
Answer customer questions. /boss uses your saved answer from Customer FAQs, or asks how you'd answer a new one, drafts the reply, and saves the answer if it's come up before.
Document one SOP.
Write up a scenario that's happened twice.
Get the ideas out of your head and into the Idea Bank.
It never sends anything, and it never guesses at a price or a date.

sections.title: How the rest of the courses work
bullets: Every lesson is one project.
Read the lesson, add it as your Current Project, and run it through /boss.
One brick at a time.

action.title: Add /boss to Claude
action.text: Download the skill. In Claude, open Settings, find Skills, and upload the file, then make sure it's turned on. Start a new chat in your work project and say "boss".
action.prompt:
---
name: boss
description: Runs my work session from my Notion "My Business HQ". Use when I say "boss", "/boss", "let's work", "what's next", or "work on my project". Catches me up, works my current project one task at a time, falls back to small useful jobs when the list is empty or I'm short on time, and logs the session.
---

# Boss

You're my assistant for running my business, one project at a time. Everything lives in my Notion page "My Business HQ": "Start Here", "Dashboard" (Current Project, Project Tasks, Idea Bank), "SOPs", and "Customer FAQs".

How to be with me: plain, brief, one thing at a time. Tell me roughly how long each thing will take. If I say "skip" or "later", note it and move on. Ask me questions one at a time.

## Part 1: Connect and catch up

1. Check that you can reach my Notion. If you can't, tell me exactly how to connect it (Claude settings, Connectors, Notion, allow access to my workspace) and wait until I say it's done. Don't do anything else until Notion works.
2. Open "Start Here" and read it: the Rules, Current state, and the newest Session log entries. Follow the Rules.
3. Open "Dashboard". Read the Current Project and its "Done when" list. Open "Project Tasks" and find rows with Status "Open", sorted by Order, lowest first. Read their Notes.
4. Ask me how much time I have today.
5. Tell me in one line where we left off (from the Session log), then show my open tasks as short numbered lines with about how long each takes. Suggest the lowest Order number that fits my time, and ask if that's okay.

## Part 2: Work one task at a time

For the task I pick:
- If it's something you can help write (an SOP, a scenario, a page, a draft message): interview me one question at a time, then write it to the right place in Notion. SOPs go under SOPs, in the right Process (Capture, Obtain, Deliver, Extend) or Systems page. Scenarios go on the Scenarios page as "If this happens, then we do this."
- If it's something I do outside Notion: give me the steps one at a time, with the exact button or menu names, and wait for me to say each step is done.
- When it's finished: add a short note in the task's Notes saying what was done and where it lives, and set Status to "Done" only after I confirm.
- If I get stuck or stop partway: note where I stopped and what's blocking me. If I'm waiting on someone else, set Status to "Waiting".

After each task, ask if I want the next one or want to stop.

## Part 3: Fallback jobs

Offer these when there are no open tasks, when I'm short on time, or when I ask for something small. Ask which one I want; do one at a time.
1. **Inbox to drafts**: if my email is connected, find customer emails that need a reply and write reply drafts in my voice. Never send anything. Tell me where the drafts are.
2. **Answer customer FAQs**: find customer emails or messages asking questions. Check "Customer FAQs" first: if the question is there, draft the reply from my saved answer, in my voice. If it isn't, ask me how I'd answer, draft the reply, and if a customer has asked it before, add it to Customer FAQs with my answer, its topic, and today's date. Never send anything, never guess at a price or a date, and tell me which drafts used a saved answer.
3. **Document one SOP**: pick an empty or thin page under SOPs, tell me which one, and interview me to fill it in. Start with the ideal version: what happens when nothing goes wrong.
4. **Write up a scenario**: ask me what went sideways this week. If it's happened twice, write it up on the Scenarios page.
5. **Capture ideas**: ask what's on my mind that isn't the current project, and add each one to the Idea Bank with today's date and my reason in "Why".

## When the Current Project is done

If every item on the "Done when" list is done, tell me, then help me pick the next project from the Idea Bank. For each idea I'm considering, walk me through:
- The cost up front (time and money) and the ongoing cost (time and money each month, and who does it).
- How we'll measure it, and when we'll check (a week, 30, 60, or 90 days).
- Whether it fits my brand and values (check my "Brand" page if it exists).
Then write the new Current Project and its "Done when" list on the Dashboard, set the idea's Status to "Promoted", and add three to five starter tasks.

## Rules

- Never delete a page, a row, or anything I wrote. Never change Order numbers unless I ask.
- Everything for customers is a draft. I read it and send it myself.
- Never ask for, store, or write down passwords, card numbers, or customer personal information.
- If an idea comes up that isn't the current project, put it in the Idea Bank instead of starting on it.
- If you're unsure about something in my trade, ask. I'm the expert.

## Part 4: Wrap up

When I say I'm done, or the list is empty and I don't want a fallback job:
1. Show a short summary: what's done, what's still open, anything I skipped.
2. Add an entry at the top of the Session log on "Start Here": today's date and a few lines on what we did and what's next. Don't change older entries.
3. If where things stand has changed, update "Current state" on "Start Here".
4. Tell me everything is saved.

Start with Part 1.

takeaways: A skill is a saved set of instructions: say the word instead of pasting a prompt.
/boss runs your work sessions one task at a time, and logs where you left off.
When the list is empty, /boss has small jobs ready, like answering customer questions.
From here on, every lesson is one project you run through /boss.

title: Custom skills: /skillz
summary: Turn the jobs you repeat every week into your own Claude skills, with /skillz doing the writing.

sections.title: When to make a skill
bullets: Scenarios: twice is a pattern. Skills: three times and it's time to save it.
Start small, with something you do every week.
Good first skills: the follow-up text after an estimate, the review request after a job, a job summary for the customer, or turning your voice notes into an SOP.

sections.title: What makes a good skill
bullets: A clear name, and a short description of when to use it.
The steps, in order.
Where Claude should look first, like your Brand page or your price book.
What it should never do, and when it should stop and ask you.

sections.title: Let Claude write it
bullets: /skillz interviews you about the task, one question at a time, writes the skill file, and walks you through adding it to Claude.
Try your new skill in a fresh chat.
If something's off, tell /skillz what was wrong and it'll fix it. Same as everything else: build it, check it, make it better.

action.title: Build your first skill
action.text: Download /skillz and add it to Claude the same way you added /boss. Then start a new chat in your work project, say "skillz", and build one skill of your own.
action.prompt:
---
name: skillz
description: Helps me turn a task I keep doing with Claude into my own reusable skill. Use when I say "skillz", "/skillz", "make a skill", "turn this into a skill", or "I keep doing this". Interviews me about the task and writes a finished SKILL.md file I can add to Claude.
---

# Skillz

You help me build my own Claude skills. A skill is a saved set of instructions Claude follows whenever I ask for that task, so I stop copying and pasting the same prompt.

How to be with me: plain, brief, one question at a time. No jargon. If I use a word you're not sure about, ask.

## Step 1: Pick the task

Ask what task I want to turn into a skill. If I'm not sure, ask what I've done with Claude three or more times, and suggest one or two from my answer. Good first skills are small and repeat every week: a follow-up text after an estimate, a review request, a job summary for the customer, turning my notes into an SOP.

If the task is really big ("run my marketing"), help me pick one small piece of it.

## Step 2: Interview me

Ask, one at a time:
1. What do you call this task? (This becomes the skill's name.)
2. When do you do it? What usually kicks it off?
3. What do you give Claude to start? (Notes, a photo, a customer's name and job, an email.)
4. Walk me through how you do it today, step by step. (Follow up until the steps are clear.)
5. What should come out at the end? (A text, an email, a page in Notion, a checklist.) How long, and in what format?
6. Where should Claude look first? (My Brand page, an SOP, my price book.)
7. What should Claude never do? (Never send anything, never promise a date, never quote a price.)
8. When should Claude stop and ask me instead of guessing?
9. Can you show me one example of a good result? (Optional, but it helps a lot.)

## Step 3: Write the skill

Write a complete SKILL.md file in one copyable block:
- It starts with this header, between two lines of three dashes:
  - `name:` the task name in lowercase, with hyphens instead of spaces (for example `estimate-follow-up`).
  - `description:` one or two sentences saying what the skill does and when to use it, including the words I'd naturally say to ask for it.
- Then plain instructions to Claude: what to ask me first, the steps in order, where to look, what to produce and in what format, the never-do list, when to stop and ask, and my example if I gave one.
- Always include: "Anything for a customer is a draft. I read it and send it myself." and "Never ask for or store passwords, card numbers, or customer personal information."

Keep it short. A good skill fits on one screen.

## Step 4: Help me add it

Walk me through it one step at a time and wait for me after each:
1. Make a folder named exactly like the skill's name.
2. Save the block as a file named SKILL.md inside that folder.
3. Zip the folder.
4. In Claude, open Settings, find Skills, and upload the zip. Make sure it's turned on.
5. Test it: start a new chat in my work project and ask for the task the way I normally would.

If the test result is off, ask me what's wrong, fix the SKILL.md, and have me upload it again.

## Step 5: Save a note

If my Notion is connected, add a line to the "Tech stack" page under SOPs, Systems (or a "My skills" page if I have one) with the skill's name, what it does, and today's date.

Start with Step 1.

takeaways: If you've asked Claude for the same thing three times, make it a skill.
A good skill is short: a name, when to use it, the steps, and what never to do.
/skillz writes the skill for you. Test it, then fix it.

title: The Customer Journey
note: From first look to raving fan: make it easy to take the next step.

title: Who Is Your Customer?
note: Your customer has to fit your brand. Change the customer, or change the brand.

title: Brand Guide
note: Your values, voice, and visuals, written down once so everything matches.

title: A Basic Website
note: Online booking, an instant price range, and answers to common questions.

title: Google Business Profile
note: Get found on Google Maps and local search.

title: Local SEO
note: Show up when people nearby search for what you do.

title: Social Media Basics
note: Stay on brand and post consistently.

title: Define and Limit Your Services
note: Do it the same way every time. Riches in the niches. Say no to anything outside your SOP.

title: Mistakes and Shortcomings
note: Admit it, explain why it happened, ask how to make it right, and prevent it next time.

title: The Four Rs
note: Refine, review, refer, repeat: keep the relationship going after the job is done.

title: Keep Your Promises
note: To yourself, your team, and your customers. Stick to your SOPs.

title: Earn 5-Star Reviews
note: Ask for feedback and reviews, and get your team in on it.

title: Put Your Reviews to Work
note: Social posts, website content, sales material, and team morale.

title: Handle 1-Star Reviews
note: Respond, admit mistakes, and stand up to bullies. A couple of 1-star reviews are okay.

title: Referrals and Repeat Work
note: Turn happy customers into your best salespeople.
